events.title: The Back Seat
events.body: The car is where he does his real business, because the car is the only room in {diocese} with one door. You drive, and he sits behind you with the phone, and he has long since stopped pretending you cannot hear. This week it is the vicar for clergy on the line, and the subject is a pastor in the north of the diocese who is going to be moved by summer and does not know it. The reasons are not scandalous; they are the ordinary reasons, a parish that has stopped growing and a man who has stopped noticing. It is {@brother_priest}. You know him. He gave you a bed the week you were ordained, and he calls the residence every few weeks to ask how the bishop is, which is his way of asking how he is. On Thursday he calls again, and asks, lightly, whether there is anything in the wind about the north, and you have the phone in your hand and the bishop is upstairs.
events.flavorPrompt: The car with one door, the phone that is not private, the pastor who calls to ask how the bishop is.

choices.label: Tell him you hear nothing in the car, and mean it
choices.outcome: You say the car is loud and the bishop keeps his own counsel, which is a lie and a courtesy at once. He accepts it because he wants to. In June the letter reaches him the way letters do. He never asks whether you knew, which is the kindest thing he could do, and you are not sure he does it on purpose.

choices.label: Tell him to start looking at the summer with an open mind
choices.outcome: You say nothing that could be quoted, and he hears all of it. He has three months to grieve a parish in private, which is a mercy, and to call two friends on the personnel board, which is not. The vicar for clergy notices that the north is expecting something. He mentions it to the bishop. The bishop does not mention it to you, and you drive in a longer silence.

choices.label: Tell the bishop that the man is calling, and that he deserves to hear it from him
choices.outcome: He looks at you over the top of the newspaper for a long moment. Then he says that you are right, and that he had been putting it off, and that he will drive north on Tuesday, and that you will drive him. The conversation in the rectory takes an hour. On the way home he says, to the window, that he should have done it a month ago.

events.title: Ten Minutes
events.body: Every priest in {diocese} has learned that the way to the bishop is through you. The calendar is yours, the phone is yours, and the ten minutes at the end of the day when he is tired enough to say yes are, in practice, yours to give. {@brother_priest} knows this. He has a school with a year left in it and a chancery that has already decided, and he has written the letters and sat through the meeting and been told that the process is the process. Now he is on the porch of the residence at seven in the evening with a folder, because he heard you might be able to get him in. He is not asking you to argue his case. He is asking for ten minutes that the chancellor would not give him, and he is asking as a man who once drove three hours to hear your first Mass. The bishop is in the study. He has had a long day. He would see him if you asked.
events.flavorPrompt: The porch at seven, the folder, the ten minutes that belong to the secretary and to no one else.

choices.label: Take him up to the study and give him his ten minutes
choices.outcome: The bishop is gracious and hears him for half an hour. Nothing changes about the school, because the numbers are the numbers, but the man leaves knowing he was heard by the one person who mattered. The chancellor learns of it by Friday and understands that the calendar has a side door. He does not raise it with you. He raises it with the bishop.

choices.label: Tell him, kindly, that the calendar is the calendar and the process is the process
choices.outcome: He takes it standing up and goes back to his car with the folder. The chancellor never learns that there was anything to learn. The school closes in June, as it would have. At the next deanery dinner the man is civil to you, in the way priests are civil to the chancery, and you understand that you have moved, in his mind, from one side of a line to the other.

choices.label: Send him home, read the folder yourself, and put the case to the bishop in three sentences
choices.outcome: The folder is better than the chancery said it was, and you tell the bishop so over the coffee at ten, with the one number that matters. He asks for the file. The school gets a year's reprieve and a condition attached to it. The pastor never knows quite how it happened, and the chancellor knows exactly, and both of them adjust their opinion of you.

events.title: The Kitchen
events.body: Three sisters keep the residence: the cooking, the linen, the chapel, and a kind of order that the bishop has never once had to think about, which is the point of it. The eldest has been here thirty-one years and four bishops. She finds you in the kitchen on a Tuesday, with the door shut, and tells you that the congregation is withdrawing them. There are not enough sisters left to keep a house like this. The provincial's letter will go to the bishop next week. She would like him to hear it from a person first, and she has decided that the person is you, because she has watched you for a year and thinks you will do it properly. She does not cry. She says the younger two do not know yet, and would you please not tell them, and that there is a roast in for six. The bishop is upstairs with the auditor and will come down hungry and in a good mood.
events.flavorPrompt: The kitchen door shut, the roast at six, thirty-one years handed over in a single sentence.

choices.label: Tell him tonight, after the roast, in the study
choices.outcome: He puts his fork down and says nothing for long enough that you wonder if you have done it wrong. Then he asks whether she is all right, which is the right first question, and goes down to the kitchen himself. You do not follow. The provincial's letter arrives on Thursday and finds a house that already knows. She sends you a card at Christmas for years.

choices.label: Let the letter come; it is the provincial's news to give, not yours
choices.outcome: The letter comes and he reads it at breakfast and is quiet for the day. She serves the lunch as if nothing has happened. Later he asks whether you knew, and you say she had told you, and he nods, and it is not an argument, only a small thing put on a shelf. You spend the spring finding a housekeeper and a caterer and a way to keep a chapel without anyone to keep it.

choices.label: Tell him tonight, and by morning have a plan: a Mass, a dinner, the priests who owe them
choices.outcome: The Mass is in the cathedral on a June evening, the bishop presiding and forty priests concelebrating, and the eldest sister in the front pew refusing to be looked at. The dinner afterward is in the residence and she does not cook it, which she takes badly. The provincial writes to the bishop that she has never seen a house say goodbye properly. The bishop tells her who arranged it.

events.title: The Oils
events.body: The Chrism Mass is the one morning of the year when the whole presbyterate of {diocese} is in one building, in white, watching. You are master of ceremonies. You have walked it twice and written it out and briefed the deacons and the servers and the cathedral sacristan, who has done this for twenty years and does not need briefing and let you know it. And now the Gloria is ending and you can see, from your place at the bishop's elbow, that the table with the vessels of oil is bare. The sacristan has the oils in the sacristy, because that is where they were last year, before the renovation. The deacon of the Word has the wrong book open. The bishop has not noticed either thing and is about to sit for the readings. Three hundred priests are in the nave, and some of them are the men who write to the nuncio, and all of them know a Chrism Mass when they see one. You have perhaps ninety seconds before the first reading and four minutes before it matters.
events.flavorPrompt: The bare table, the wrong book, the ninety seconds at the bishop's elbow with the whole presbyterate watching.

choices.label: Send a server for the oils during the readings and swap the book at the Alleluia
choices.outcome: The server goes and comes back with the vessels under a humeral veil he found, which was quick thinking and wrong, and the book is swapped while everyone stands. Nobody in the nave sees a thing. The bishop, afterward, asks why the deacon looked so frightened, and you tell him, and he laughs. The sacristan does not speak to you until Pentecost.

choices.label: Step to the bishop, tell him, and let him pause the Mass for a minute in front of everyone
choices.outcome: He stands, says into the microphone that we will wait a moment for the oils, and sits down again, and three hundred priests are given a minute to understand exactly whose job that was. The oils come. The Mass is beautiful. At lunch four pastors tell you, kindly, that it happens to everyone, which is how you learn that it will be told for years.

choices.label: Move the renewal of priestly promises forward and bring the oils in procession after it, as if it were planned
choices.outcome: It is not the order in the book, but it is an order, and the rubrics allow more than the sacristan thinks. The promises are renewed, and then the oils come up the aisle carried by three deacons, and the effect is better than the book. Two pastors ask you afterward where the procession came from. One monsignor knows exactly, and tells the bishop, and the bishop looks at you differently.

effects.key: saved a Chrism Mass without anyone seeing

events.title: The Study at Eleven
events.body: The day was a funeral in the morning, for a priest he ordained, and a meeting with the lawyers in the afternoon about a file from 1988, and a dinner with the finance council at which the numbers did not improve. You drove all of it. At eleven the house is dark except for the study, and he calls you in as you pass, and there is a bottle on the desk that was full at nine. He is not drunk in any way a stranger would see. He is drunk in the way you have learned to see, three nights this month, which is a slowness in the hands and a willingness to talk about 1988. He wants you to sit. He says it is nothing. He says that in the old days a bishop had a house full of priests and now he has a secretary and three sisters, and he laughs, and pours, and there is a second glass on the tray that he has clearly put there for you.

choices.label: Sit, and let him talk, and say nothing about the bottle
choices.outcome: You sit until one. He talks about 1988 and about the man he buried and about a seminary in Ohio forty years ago. You do not drink. He notices that you do not, and does not remark on it, and at one he stands up steadily enough and says goodnight. In the morning he is the bishop again, and the study smells of nothing, and neither of you mentions it.

choices.label: Say goodnight, take the tray to the kitchen, and leave him the room
choices.outcome: He watches you pick it up and says nothing, which is the most frightening thing he has ever said to you. In the morning he is early to the chapel and short with the sisters. It is a week before he speaks to you about anything but the calendar. The bottle does not appear on the desk again while you are in the house, and you will never know whether that was you or him.

effects.key: took the bottle off his bishop's desk

choices.label: Sit down, and tell him it is the third night this month, and that you are worried
choices.outcome: He is quiet for a long time. Then he says that his own secretary told him the same thing in another diocese, twenty years ago, and that he did not listen then. He does not promise anything. He asks you to keep the evenings clear after nine for a month, and to come and sit whether there is a bottle or not. There is not, mostly. He does not forget that you said it.

effects.key: told his bishop the truth at eleven at night

events.title: In His Name
events.body: {@brother_priest} preached on Sunday about the diocese, and specifically about a decision of the bishop's, and specifically that it was wrong, and someone recorded it, and by Tuesday the bishop has heard it twice. He is not shouting. He is dictating, at the desk, in the flat voice he uses for things he has already decided: a letter to the man, formal, on the letterhead, reminding him of the promise he made at ordination with his hands in a bishop's hands. Then he stops and says, write it up, you know what I mean, and goes to a meeting. You know what he means. You also know the man, who is not a rebel but a pastor who watched a school close, and you know that a letter on the letterhead goes in a file and a file is forever. The chancellor, passing, asks whether he can see it before it goes. The bishop wants it on his desk by five.
events.flavorPrompt: The dictation in the flat voice, the letterhead, the file that is forever, five o'clock.

choices.label: Write it as he meant it, on the letterhead, with the promise in it
choices.outcome: He reads it once, signs it, and says it is good, which he does not say. The letter goes by hand. The pastor does not preach about the diocese again, and does not preach about anything with much heart for a year. The chancellor notes that you can write a letter that lands. So do the priests of the diocese, who hear about it, and remember the hand it came from.

choices.label: Write two versions, one as he meant it and one as a phone call would go, and put both on the desk
choices.outcome: He reads both and is annoyed for a minute and then is not. He makes the phone call. It takes twenty minutes and ends with the pastor apologizing, which the letter would never have got. Nothing goes in a file. The chancellor, who wanted the letter, files instead a small note about the secretary. You have learned that a bishop can be given a choice if it is given to him quietly.

choices.label: Call the pastor before you write a word, and tell him what is coming and what to do about it
choices.outcome: He is at the residence by four with a letter of his own, handwritten, and the bishop reads it before yours is finished and tears yours up. It is a good afternoon for two of the three men involved. The third is the chancellor, who was told nothing and understands that the secretary has his own lines. The bishop never asks how the pastor knew.

events.title: Two in the Morning
events.body: The residence phone rings at ten past two and you have it before the second ring, because that is the job. It is {@brother_priest}, and he is on the shoulder of the county road with a state trooper's lights behind him, and he has been drinking, and the car is in a ditch and nobody is hurt, and he wants the bishop. He says it three times. He is not asking for help. He is asking to be the one who tells him, before the trooper's report reaches the chancery by the ordinary route on Monday, and he is crying in the way men cry when they are more frightened of a letter than of a judge. The bishop is asleep upstairs and has a Mass at seven and a confirmation at ten. The vicar for clergy has a phone and a job that this is. You have a car, and the road is forty minutes, and the man on the phone has stopped talking and is waiting to hear what you will do.

choices.label: Wake the bishop; it is his priest, and he would want to know tonight
choices.outcome: He comes down in his dressing gown and takes the phone and talks for ten minutes in a voice you have not heard him use. Then he tells you to drive out. You do. The bishop is at the seven o'clock Mass looking as if he has slept. On Monday there is a meeting, and a program, and a leave, and none of it is a surprise to anyone, which is the mercy in it.

choices.label: Tell him you are coming, drive out, and let the bishop hear it from you at breakfast
choices.outcome: You are there by three. The trooper is decent about it. You drive the man home and sit in his kitchen until it is light and he is asleep in the chair. The bishop hears it over coffee and is quiet, and then asks why you did not wake him, and you say the man needed a priest first and a bishop second. He does not disagree. He does not entirely like it.

choices.label: Give him the vicar for clergy's number; that is what the office is for
choices.outcome: He says nothing for a moment and then says thank you, Father, in a voice with a door closing in it, and hangs up. The vicar for clergy handles it, competently, by the book. The bishop hears on Monday and thinks nothing of it. The man does not call the residence again, and when you meet him at the Chrism Mass he shakes your hand exactly as he shakes everyone's.

events.title: The Confirmation Tour
events.body: From Easter to Pentecost the bishop confirms in a different parish four evenings a week, and you drive, and vest him, and stand at his elbow with the chrism, and eat forty parish suppers. By the fifth week he is grey with it. Tonight is a parish where the confirmation class is sixty-one young people, two-thirds of them with parents who speak Spanish at home, and the pastor takes you aside in the sacristy with a request. The bishop's Spanish is phonetic; he reads it from a card, and he reads it well, but the homily is in English and half the church will get it from their children afterward. Would Father, the pastor asks, meaning you, consider doing the Spanish parts, the greeting and a word after the homily, so that the parents hear something in their own language from someone who means it. The bishop is in the sacristy chair with his eyes shut. The organ has started. It is a small thing, and it is also his Mass.
events.flavorPrompt: The fifth week of the tour, the grey bishop in the sacristy chair, the pastor's request whispered over the organ.

choices.label: Ask the bishop, and do the Spanish parts yourself
choices.outcome: He opens his eyes and says yes, go ahead, in the tone of a man being handed something heavy. The greeting is yours and the word after the homily is yours, and the parents hear it, and afterward a grandmother holds your hands for a long time and tells the bishop, in Spanish, that this one is good. He asks you to translate. You do, mostly.

choices.label: Tell the pastor the bishop will do it as he does it everywhere, and let him
choices.outcome: He reads the card well, as he always does, and the parents are gracious, as they always are, and the pastor is polite to you at supper in the way of a man who asked for something small and was refused. The bishop does not know a thing was asked. In the car he says the parish was warm, and it was, and you say nothing about what it might have been.

choices.label: Find the parish's deacon, who is from Guanajuato, and put him on the microphone after the homily
choices.outcome: The deacon is terrified and then is not, and says a word in Spanish that goes on somewhat longer than a word, and the church answers him. The bishop, who did not expect it, takes it well and thanks the deacon by name at the end. The pastor is grateful. You have learned that the job is mostly finding the right person and putting them where the microphone is.

events.title: Before She Stops Coming
events.body: She has been at the Sunday night Mass every week for three years, in the second pew on the left, and she has lectored and made the coffee and once drove a freshman to the emergency room at four in the morning. She comes to the open door on a Wednesday and shuts it behind her and says she is leaving the Church. She wants you to hear it from her and not from the empty pew. The reasons are the reasons: a professor, a book, the way a bishop somewhere answered a question, and under all of it a thing she cannot say and you can see, which is that she has stopped being able to pray and has decided that this means something. She is not angry. She is sad and precise, the way a good student is precise. She says she is grateful for the Center and for you. She says she does not want to be argued with, and then she waits, because some part of her does.

choices.label: Argue with her, carefully, because she came here to be argued with
choices.outcome: You take the professor and the book apart in twenty minutes, which is easy, and then you reach the thing underneath and cannot touch it. She listens to all of it and thanks you and goes. She does not come back to Mass. A year later she emails you from a city you have never been to, and says she is still thinking about what you said, and that is all she says.

choices.label: Tell her the door is not locked, bless her, and let her go
choices.outcome: You say that the pew will be there and so will you, and you bless her, and she cries for the first time, and then she goes. The second pew is empty on Sunday and for many Sundays. In the spring she is at the Easter Vigil, at the back, and leaves before the end. You do not go after her. You have learned that the door being unlocked is most of what you have to offer.

choices.label: Ask her for one thing: the discussion series, one more term, no Mass required
choices.outcome: She says that is a trick, and you say yes, and she comes anyway, on Tuesdays, and sits with the atheist and argues with the sophomores, and says nothing about God to you for four months. In May she asks whether the chapel is open in the afternoons. It is. You do not ask what she does there. The second pew stays empty; the chapel does not.

events.title: He Wants to Be a Priest
events.body: He is a junior, twenty, received into the Church at last year's Vigil, and he has not missed a daily Mass since. He reads more than the seminarians you were ordained with. He fasts on Fridays in a way that worries the cook. He comes to the open door and says, without sitting down, that he wants to go to seminary for {diocese} and he wants you to write the letter, because you are the priest who knows him. You do know him. You know that he is bright and generous and that he was baptized fourteen months ago and that there is something in his fervor that has not yet been tested by a bad year, and that the vocations director, who is a good man, will see a convert with a Newman Center chaplain's letter and a shortage, and will say yes. You also know that {diocese} needs him, or needs someone, and that men have gone to seminary at twenty with less and come out priests. He is waiting. He has already told his parents.
events.flavorPrompt: The junior standing in the doorway, the fourteen months since the Vigil, the letter that would be believed.

choices.label: Write the letter, warmly, and let the seminary do its work
choices.outcome: The vocations director calls to thank you, and the man enters in August, and the seminary does its work: he is sent home after the second year, kindly, with a recommendation to come back in five. He does not come back. He teaches high school in another state and is, by his Christmas cards, a good man and a practicing Catholic. The vocations director never mentions it. Neither do you.

choices.label: Tell him to finish the degree and come back to you in two years, and that the answer is not no
choices.outcome: He takes it badly for a week and then takes it. He finishes the degree. He has a bad year, the one you knew was coming, and comes through it, and comes to see you in the spring of it looking older. Two years later a different chaplain writes his letter, and it is a better letter than yours would have been, because there is more to say.

choices.label: Take him on yourself: an hour a week for a year, and then you will write whatever is true
choices.outcome: It is a year of Thursdays. He stops fasting and starts eating with people. He gets angry at God once, properly, in your office, and is embarrassed, and you tell him that was the first useful thing he has said. In May you write the letter, and it is a long one, and the vocations director reads it twice and calls you to ask where you learned to write a letter like that.

events.title: The Speaker
events.body: The faculty senate's spring lecture is a biologist with a book, and the book's argument is that religious formation of children is a species of harm, and the poster has a chalice on it. The Catholic students have found this out and want you to do something. Six of them are in your office with a draft letter to the student newspaper, and two of them want to stand outside the hall with signs. The dean of students has already called to say, in the voice of a woman who has been told to call, that the university values the chaplaincy and hopes it will respect academic freedom. The lecture is Thursday. There will be a question period. You have read the book, which is worse than its reviews and better than the students think, and you have a collar, and the room will be six hundred people, most of whom have never heard a priest ask a question. The students are waiting for you to say what the Center is going to do.
events.flavorPrompt: The chalice on the poster, the six students with the draft letter, the dean's careful voice, the microphone in the aisle.

choices.label: Go, sit in the front, and ask him one question that he cannot answer
choices.outcome: The question is about his own chapter four and its own data, and it takes forty seconds to ask, and he takes three minutes not to answer it. The room notices. The student paper runs it. The biologist is gracious afterward and says he would like to have coffee, and does, and you have a friend on the faculty who does not believe a word you say and reads everything you send him.

choices.label: Write the students' letter yourself, under your own name, and let them carry the signs
choices.outcome: The column runs on Wednesday and is read by everyone who reads the student paper and by the dean, who reads it twice. The signs are polite. The lecture goes on. The Catholic students are proud of you in the way that fills a chapel for a month, and the faculty who tolerated a priest at their table are cooler for a year. The bishop's office receives a clipping, sent by someone, with no note.

choices.label: Tell the students the Center does not picket lectures, and hold a discussion of the book on Tuesday instead
choices.outcome: Two of the six are disgusted with you and say so. The Tuesday discussion is the best attended of the year, because the atheist brings the biology department. The dean writes a note thanking you for your professionalism, which you file. Nobody outside the campus hears anything. The chalice on the poster is still on the poster, and you walk past it every day for a month.

events.title: The Man Who Pays for the Building
events.body: The Center's building was paid for by one man, an alumnus with a construction firm and a wife who died young, and his name is on the lintel, and his check comes every January and is most of the budget. He attends the Sunday night Mass twice a year, in a suit, and this year he stays afterward and asks for a word in your office. He does not like the music. He says it kindly and at length: the guitar, the songs from the seventies, the students in shorts. He was formed by a different Church and he paid for this building so that there would be somewhere on campus where that Church still stood. He would like the guitar gone and a hymnal and, ideally, some Latin, and he would like it by Advent. He does not say what happens in January if it is not. He does not have to. The students who play the guitar are the same students who run the food pantry and drove the freshman to the hospital, and they have never met him.
events.flavorPrompt: The name on the lintel, the January check, the guitar that belongs to the students who do everything.

choices.label: Give him the music: a hymnal by Advent, the guitar retired, a Latin ordinary once a month
choices.outcome: The students who play the guitar stop coming to the Sunday night Mass and go to the parish in town, and the food pantry loses two of its four people. The Mass is quieter and, in a way you do not say aloud, better. The check comes in January with a note. Some of the students call it the donor's Mass, and they are not wrong, and you are the one saying it.

choices.label: Tell him, kindly and at length, that the music is the students', and that you will take what comes in January
choices.outcome: He listens all the way through and shakes your hand and leaves. January comes and the check is half. The bishop's office notices the budget and calls to ask what happened, and you tell them, and they say nothing useful. The students never know how close it was. The guitar is terrible and you have never been so glad to hear it.

choices.label: Take him to dinner, and find him a second thing to build: a chapel where his Church can stand
choices.outcome: Over the third course he talks about his wife, and by the coffee you have a plan for the unused room at the back: a small chapel, a proper altar, adoration on Thursdays, a Latin Mass on first Fridays said by a priest from town who knows the rite. He pays for all of it and comes on first Fridays. The guitar stays. The bishop hears that the Center has a new chapel and a donor who is happy.

events.title: The Chapel Schedule
events.body: The dean of students is a decent woman with a job that mostly consists of being decent to people who want incompatible things, and today she wants something from you. The campus chapel, where the Sunday night Mass has been said since before either of you was born, is to become a multifaith space. There will be a schedule. The Catholic Mass will keep its Sunday evening, probably, and lose the weekday noon Mass and the Thursday adoration, and the tabernacle will need to be, she says, relocated, and she uses the word as if it were a piece of furniture. She is not hostile. She has a Muslim student association without a room and a Hindu one without anything, and a provost. She would like the chaplain's cooperation, which she says is valued, and she would like it in writing by the end of the month. The students do not know yet. The bishop does not know yet. The chapel was given to the university in 1927 by a Catholic family, and you have wondered, once or twice, what the deed says.
events.flavorPrompt: The dean's decency, the word relocated, the 1927 deed nobody has read.

choices.label: Refuse to sign, tell the students, and let the university hear from three hundred of them
choices.outcome: The students are magnificent and unreasonable and the provost's inbox fills. The tabernacle stays. The noon Mass stays. The Muslim students get a room in the library basement and their president, who is a friend of two of yours, does not speak to the Center for a year. The dean is professional with you forever after, which is not the same as friendly. The bishop's office hears that the chaplain can raise a crowd.

choices.label: Negotiate: the tabernacle stays in a side chapel, the noon Mass moves to the Center, the rest is theirs
choices.outcome: It takes six meetings and a floor plan, and in the end everyone has less than they wanted and something they can use. The side chapel is small and always has someone in it. The Muslim students bring you dates at Ramadan. Some of the Catholic students think you gave the building away, and say so in the parish in town, and it gets back to the bishop as a question rather than a complaint.

choices.label: Spend a week in the county records, and bring the dean the deed of 1927
choices.outcome: The deed reserves the building for Catholic worship in perpetuity, in the handwriting of a lawyer who anticipated exactly this meeting, and the university's own counsel reads it and closes the folder. The dean is relieved, in the end, to have been told no by a document rather than a priest. The multifaith space goes elsewhere. Nobody on campus knows why, and you make sure of that.

events.title: The Vigil
events.body: A sophomore is found in his room on a Sunday morning, and by noon the whole campus knows, and by two the university has decided on a vigil for Monday night on the main lawn. The dean calls you, because you are the chaplain the students actually know, and asks you to lead it. There are conditions, which she gives you gently: it will be for everyone, so there is to be no mention of God by name, no scripture, no prayer that is a prayer, and a poem would be welcome. Candles are fine. The boy was Catholic. His roommate has been in your office twice already and cannot stop talking, and his parents are driving nine hours and have asked, through the roommate, whether Father would say a Mass. The university would prefer the Mass to be private and on another night. Two thousand students will be on the lawn on Monday, most of whom have never been to a funeral, and they will be looking at whoever holds the microphone.
events.flavorPrompt: The lawn on Monday night, the candles, the microphone with conditions on it, the parents nine hours away.

choices.label: Lead the vigil as the university asks, and give them everything but the name
choices.outcome: You say what can be said without the name, and it is a great deal, and you say it well, and two thousand candles go up. The dean weeps. The parents are on the lawn, having driven straight there, and afterward the mother asks why you did not pray, and you tell her, and she nods and does not understand. The Mass is Tuesday in the Center, with sixty people, and it is the better night.

choices.label: Take the microphone, and say the boy's name and God's, and pray, and let the university do what it likes
choices.outcome: You say the Our Father on the lawn and perhaps a third of two thousand say it with you, and the rest are silent in a way that is not hostile. The dean does not weep. The provost's office sends a letter, which you keep. The parents hold you afterward and do not let go. Three students come to the open door that week to ask about the thing you said, and stay.

effects.key: prayed aloud on the lawn when he was asked not to

choices.label: Decline the lawn, and announce a Mass in the chapel at the same hour for anyone who wants one
choices.outcome: The university finds a counselor for the microphone and the lawn goes ahead. The chapel is full past the doors, four hundred at least, most of them not Catholic and none of them sure where to sit. You preach the resurrection to people who have never heard it preached. The dean is hurt. The parents are at the front. The two events are talked about for a year as if they had been a contest, which you did not intend.

events.title: The Petition
events.body: Twenty-three students have signed it, which on this campus is a movement. They want a Latin Mass at the Center. They have not agreed among themselves what they mean by that: four of them mean the old rite and have been driving forty minutes to a chapel to get it, a dozen mean the Mass they already have but in Latin, with chant and the priest facing the altar, and the rest signed because a friend asked. The one who brings it to you is the president of the student council and an engineer and entirely sincere. He says the Center should have something that feels like the Church and not like a youth group. He is not wrong about the youth group. He is also, you can see, the kind of young man who will be in a different parish in five years if he does not get this, and in a chapel of his own by thirty if he does. {@bishop} has a policy on all of this, and a temper about it, and a secretary who reads the campus paper.
events.flavorPrompt: The twenty-three signatures, the engineer's sincerity, the bishop's secretary reading the campus paper.

choices.label: Give them the Mass they have, in Latin, with chant and the priest facing east, once a month
choices.outcome: The first one is badly sung and full. By the third the chant is respectable and the four who wanted the old rite have stopped coming, and the dozen who wanted this have brought thirty. The campus paper runs a photograph. The bishop's secretary sees it and asks, on the phone, whether that was ad orientem, and you say yes, and there is a pause that goes in a file.

choices.label: Send the petition to the bishop with a covering letter, and do what he says
choices.outcome: He says no to the old rite, yes to Latin in the ordinary form on feast days, and adds a line about the guitar that you do not show the students. The engineer is disappointed and respects it, because it came from a bishop. Four students keep driving forty minutes. The chancery notes that the chaplain asks before he acts, which under this bishop is the whole of wisdom.

choices.label: Tell them the Center's Mass is the Center's Mass, and point the four at the chapel that has what they want
choices.outcome: The engineer thanks you for your time in a way you will hear again from parish councils. The four keep driving. Nine of the twenty-three find the parish in town, which has an organ. The Sunday night Mass is what it was, and the youth group remark stays with you longer than you expect. The bishop hears nothing, which was the point, and which is also its own kind of nothing.

choices.label: Spend the summer learning the old rite from the priest at the chapel, and offer it yourself in the fall
choices.outcome: The priest at the chapel is seventy-eight and delighted and merciless, and by September you can say a low Mass without the card. The first one is on a Friday with forty people, most of them not students. The bishop learns of it from the campus paper before he learns of it from you, which is the wrong order, and says so. The four are yours for life. So is a reputation.

events.title: Tuesdays
events.body: He came to the first discussion series of the year to argue and he has come to every one since. He is a philosophy major with a beard he is too young for and he has read more Aquinas than the Catholics in the room, and he uses it. Some Tuesdays he wins. The students who run the Center have started to dread him: he takes up half the evening, he makes the freshmen feel stupid, and last week he made a girl cry with a question about her grandmother and hell that was, you had to admit, a fair question. The missionaries who work with the Center have asked you, politely, whether he might be asked to come less. He has never once been rude to you. He stays after to help stack chairs and asks, stacking, what you actually believe about the thing you said, and listens to the answer. You are fairly sure he has nowhere else on this campus where anyone will talk to him about it.
events.flavorPrompt: The beard he is too young for, the chairs stacked after, the question about the grandmother.

choices.label: Keep him; a discussion series that cannot survive one atheist is not a discussion series
choices.outcome: The freshmen learn to answer him or to leave, and most learn to answer him. The girl with the grandmother comes back and, in November, takes him apart on the problem of evil in a way that surprises everyone including her. The missionaries are unhappy and then are not. He is at the Easter Vigil in the back row, not kneeling, watching. He tells you afterward it was well done.

choices.label: Take him aside and set terms: one question a night, and the freshmen go first
choices.outcome: He takes it seriously, being a serious person, and keeps to it. His one question is better for being one. The evenings are gentler and the freshmen talk more and the missionaries are grateful. He comes a little less by spring, and you are not sure whether that is the terms or the calendar, and he would not tell you if you asked.

choices.label: Give him an hour on Thursdays, just the two of you, and the whole of Aquinas if he wants it
choices.outcome: Thursdays become the best hour of your week and possibly of his. You read the Summa together, badly, in Latin, and argue about it, and he never once gives an inch on the existence of God and never once misses a week. On Tuesdays he is gentler with the freshmen, because he has somewhere to put the rest. Years later he sends you his dissertation. The dedication is to you.

events.title: Two Pages
events.body: The pager goes at ten to three, and then, while you are still finding your shoes, it goes again. The first is the cardiac unit on four: a man of seventy with a wife who has asked for a priest and a monitor that the nurse, in the language nurses use, describes as not good. The second is the neonatal unit on six: a baby born at twenty-six weeks whose mother is Catholic and nineteen and alone and has asked, the nurse says, whether the baby can be baptized now, and the nurse says now in a way that means now. It is one building and two elevators and you are one priest. The night supervisor, who has done this for twenty years, says on the phone that either family will understand, which is true and does not help. You have the oils and a bottle of water in the bag that is always packed. The elevator on your floor has come. It will go up or down.
events.flavorPrompt: The pager twice, the packed bag, the elevator that goes up or down.

choices.label: Go up: the baby, the water, then down to the fourth floor
choices.outcome: The baptism takes four minutes through the port of an incubator with a nurse holding the light, and the mother holds your sleeve. The man on four is dead when you arrive, eleven minutes later, and his wife is sitting with him, and you anoint him anyway, conditionally, and stay an hour. She says that he would have wanted the baby done first. You are not sure she means it. You are not sure it matters.

choices.label: Go down: the anointing, the man who can still hear you, then up
choices.outcome: He is conscious and knows what the oil is and says the responses with you, and dies twenty minutes after, with his wife's hand in his and yours on his head. On six the baby is alive and stays alive, and you baptize him at four in the morning with the mother crying and the nurse crying and the monitor beeping in time. It was the right order tonight. Another night it would not be.

choices.label: Call {@brother_priest}, whose rectory is six minutes away, and take the fourth floor yourself
choices.outcome: He answers on the third ring and is in the building in nine minutes with his hair standing up, and takes the elevator to six without a word. Both are done. Both are done well. He has coffee with you in the cafeteria at five and says that this is the first time anyone has called him for anything in a year, and that you should do it again, and you understand that he means it.

events.title: What the Doctors Cannot Do
events.body: He is fifty-four and has been on the ventilator for nineteen days and the scans have stopped changing. The attending has said, twice, in the careful words the hospital teaches, that it is time to talk about what he would have wanted. The wife will not talk about it. She has a rosary and a novena and a prayer card from a shrine, and she has decided that what he needs is a miracle and that what the doctors need is a priest to tell them so. She asks you, in the hallway, with the daughters listening, to come into the family meeting at four and to say in front of the physicians that God can heal him and that they must not stop. She is not wrong that God can. You have anointed him twice. The attending, who is Jewish and kind and has been doing this for thirty years, has asked you privately whether you might help the family understand. Both of them think you are on their side. At four you will be in a room with all of them.

choices.label: Go in, pray for a miracle aloud with the family, and say nothing to the physicians
choices.outcome: You pray, and the family prays, and the physicians stand with their hands folded and wait for it to be over. Nothing is decided. He lives eleven more days on the machine and dies on a Tuesday with the novena unfinished. The wife says at the funeral that you never gave up on him, and means it as the highest praise, and the attending nods to you in the corridor and does not ask you to a family meeting again.

choices.label: Say, in the room, what the Church actually teaches about a machine and a man
choices.outcome: You say it plainly: that no one is obliged to extraordinary means, that stopping the machine is not killing him, that God does not need a ventilator to work a miracle. The attending is grateful. The wife looks at you as if you had struck her, and does not speak to you again, and the daughters do, later, one at a time, to say thank you. He dies two days after the machine is stopped.

choices.label: Before four, sit with the wife alone, and ask her what he said he wanted, once, at a kitchen table
choices.outcome: It takes an hour and most of it is silence. Then she tells you about a conversation after her father's death, and what he said, and that she has known for a week. At four she tells the physicians herself. You say nothing at all in the meeting except the blessing at the end. The attending walks you to the elevator and says that in thirty years he has never seen that done.

events.title: The Committee
events.body: The ethics committee meets in a conference room with bad coffee, and it is the oncologist, the hospital's lawyer, a nurse, a bioethicist from the university, and you, because the hospital is Catholic and the diocese put a priest on the committee in 1994 and never took him off. The case is a woman of thirty-one, sixteen weeks pregnant, with a cancer of the uterus that will kill her by the summer if it is not removed, and cannot be removed without the pregnancy ending. The oncologist wants to operate. The lawyer wants the committee's minute to say that the Catholic chaplain agreed. The woman and her husband are in a room on three, and have asked to see you afterward, and want to know what the Church says, because they intend to do what it says. You know what it says, and the distinction it draws, and that the distinction is real and that it is also a knife. Everyone in the room is looking at you. The lawyer has a pen.

choices.label: State the teaching precisely, the principle and its limits, and let the committee minute what it likes
choices.outcome: You say it in four sentences, as it stands, and the bioethicist says that is correct, and the oncologist says thank you, and the lawyer writes. On three, you say it again to the couple, more slowly. The husband asks whether it is a sin, and you say no, and he puts his head in his hands. The surgery is Thursday. She lives. You do not sleep well for a week, and nobody on the committee asks why.

choices.label: Say the diocese has a moral theologian for exactly this, and that you will not speak for the Church alone
choices.outcome: The committee adjourns for a day and the theologian comes down from the chancery, an old priest with a briefcase, and says what you would have said, and says it better, and signs the minute himself. The couple hears it from him. The oncologist thinks less of you; the lawyer thinks more. You have learned that there are rooms in which a priest may decline to be the only priest.

choices.label: Take the room through the whole of it, the principle and the cases and where the line is and why
choices.outcome: It takes forty minutes and the bioethicist, who came to correct you, takes notes. The nurse asks a question nobody has asked her in twelve years of these meetings and you answer it. The minute says what it needs to say. The couple, on three, get the short version, and the husband says he wishes he had heard the long one, and you say he did not need to. He did not.

events.title: Three in the Morning
events.body: She works nights on the oncology floor and has for eleven years, and she is the one who pages you when it is time and the one who has the coffee ready when you come out of the room. She is forty-four and divorced and has a son at the state university, and she does not believe in much, and she is the best nurse in the building. It began as the coffee. Now it is twenty minutes in the break room after every death, and she asks how you are, which no one else in {diocese} does, and you tell her. Last week she touched your arm when she said goodnight and you have thought about it since, more than you have thought about anything, and you have started arranging your rounds so that you are on six at three in the morning whether there is a death or not. Nothing has happened. Nothing has been said. You are a priest with a vow and a friend, and she is the only person in the building who knows your first name, and it is three in the morning again.

choices.label: Keep the coffee and the twenty minutes, and keep it what it is, and trust yourself
choices.outcome: It stays what it is, for a year, and it costs you something to keep it there that you do not name. She never says anything and neither do you. When you leave the hospital she gives you a card with her son's graduation photograph in it and you keep the card. You are not sure, years later, whether that was a friendship kept or a line walked, and the not knowing is its own cost.

choices.label: Change your rounds, take the coffee from the machine, and say nothing to anyone
choices.outcome: She notices in a week and says nothing, and the break room becomes a room you pass. It is lonelier on six at three in the morning than it was, which you had not expected, and the deaths are harder without the twenty minutes. She is professional with you and kind, and once, in the elevator, says she hopes she did not do anything, and you say no, and it is true and it is not.

choices.label: Tell her, once, plainly, what you are and what you are not and why the rounds are changing
choices.outcome: She listens, and looks at the coffee for a while, and says that she had wondered, and that she is glad you said it and not her. The rounds change. The twenty minutes become five, in the corridor, in daylight, and are worth more for it. When you leave she says you are the only priest she has ever believed, which is not what you were trying for, and is what you got.

effects.key: said the hard thing to a friend at three in the morning

events.title: Room 412
events.body: {@brother_priest} is admitted on a Monday and by Thursday the oncologist has stopped talking about the summer. He is a priest of {diocese}, forty years ordained, three parishes and a chancery office and a retirement nobody thought he wanted, and he is in a room on four with a breviary he cannot hold and a nephew who comes at six. He asks for you by name. He wants confession first, and you hear it, and it takes an hour, and it is the confession of a man who has been keeping a list. Afterward he wants something else. There is a thing about the diocese, he says, from the eighties, that {@bishop} does not know and should, and he has decided that you are the one to carry it, because you will be at the residence or the chancery someday and he will not. He does not know that you know what this costs. He says it is not under the seal. He says he would like it done before Sunday, and then he sleeps.

choices.label: Sit with him until the end, and carry nothing out of the room but the memory of him
choices.outcome: You tell him, on Friday, that whatever it is should go to the bishop in his own voice or not at all, and he looks at you for a long time and says that is probably right. He dies on Sunday night with you and the nephew there. The thing from the eighties dies with him. You will wonder, in a chancery office someday, what it was, and you will be glad, mostly, that you do not know.

choices.label: Take it down, exactly, and carry it to the bishop yourself after the funeral
choices.outcome: It is four pages in your hand and he signs the last one with help. He dies on Saturday. You drive to the residence the Tuesday after the funeral and the bishop reads it in front of you, twice, and puts it in a drawer and thanks you, and asks you never to mention it, and you never do. Something in the diocese changes quietly the following year, and you are the only priest who knows why.

choices.label: Call {@closest_classmate}, who was his vicar once, and ask him to come and sit the nights with you
choices.outcome: He drives in that night and stays three, sleeping in the chair, and the old man is glad of him in a way that is visible. The three of you say Compline on Saturday with the nephew holding the book. He dies during the Nunc Dimittis, which the nephew will tell people for the rest of his life. The thing from the eighties is never mentioned again; he had, you think, only wanted to be sure someone would come.

events.title: The Proxy
events.body: He asked for you on Tuesday, when he could still ask, and you came and talked and he said he would like the anointing on Thursday when his daughter was there, because he wanted her to see it. On Thursday he cannot speak. The daughter is there. She is his health care proxy and she is fifty and she left the Church at nineteen over something she does not say, and she stands between you and the bed and says no. She says he was confused on Tuesday. She says she will not have him frightened with oil and Latin in his last hours. She is not shouting. She is a woman doing what she believes is protecting her father, and she has the paperwork, and the charge nurse is in the doorway not knowing whose side the hospital is on. He asked you. He is not confused now; he is unconscious, which is different, and his hand moved when you said his name. The oils are in your pocket. She is between you and the bed.

choices.label: Tell her he asked, step past her, and anoint him
choices.outcome: It takes ninety seconds and she does not physically stop you, and afterward she is shaking with a rage that has been waiting thirty years for something to attach to. She complains to the hospital in writing. The hospital, which is Catholic, is caught between its chaplain and its patient's proxy and finds for neither. He dies that night, anointed. She does not attend the funeral. You were right, and it cost her the last hour with her father.

choices.label: Respect the proxy, say the prayers in the hallway where she can hear them, and stay
choices.outcome: You stand in the corridor and say the commendation of the dying aloud, not loudly, and the charge nurse stands with you. The daughter can hear it and does not close the door. He dies at four in the morning. She comes out and finds you still in the chair, and sits down two chairs away, and after a while says that he would have liked that you stayed. It is not the sacrament. It is what there was.

choices.label: Ask her for twenty minutes in the family room, and ask her what happened when she was nineteen
choices.outcome: It is not twenty minutes; it is an hour and a half, and it is not about the oil. When she comes back to the room she stands by the bed and tells you to go ahead, and watches, and cries, and holds his hand through it. He dies at dawn. She does not come back to the Church, and she sends you a Christmas card every year, and one year it has a Mass card in it.

events.title: Outcomes
events.body: The new administrator is forty and came from a hospital system in another state and has a slide deck. He likes you. He says so. He also has a board, and a board has a consultant, and the consultant has determined that spiritual care is the one department in the building with no metrics, and he would like some by the end of the quarter. He is reasonable about it. Visits per shift, he suggests. Patient satisfaction scores, with a question about the chaplain. Response time on the pager. A dashboard. He says the words spiritual care as if they were a service line, which in his world they are, and he points out, correctly, that the department that cannot show its value is the department that gets cut when the system buys the hospital, which it will. He would like you to design it, because you are the one who knows what the work is. He would like a draft by Friday.
events.flavorPrompt: The slide deck, the service line, the dashboard for the thing that happens in rooms with the door shut.

choices.label: Build the dashboard, honestly, and let the numbers say what they say
choices.outcome: You log every visit for a quarter and it is a great many visits and the response time on the pager is better than any department in the building. The board is impressed. The consultant uses the department as an example. You spend forty minutes a day on the log that you used to spend on six, and the nurses notice, and say nothing, and page you a little less because they know you are busy.

choices.label: Tell him that what happens in the rooms cannot be counted, and that you will not pretend it can
choices.outcome: He is disappointed and polite and gives the job to the consultant, who invents a metric that measures nothing and puts it in the deck. The department survives the acquisition, barely, on the strength of a letter from the bishop that you did not ask for and he did not tell you he wrote. The administrator thinks you are a good priest and a bad colleague. He is not entirely wrong on either count.

choices.label: Give him numbers, but yours: sacraments, families seen, referrals to hospice and to the parishes, and what they cost
choices.outcome: The draft is three pages and it counts what a priest would count and it prices the department against the hospice referrals it produces, which is a number the board understands. The administrator reads it twice and adopts it whole. The consultant is annoyed. The department gets a second chaplain in the next budget, a lay woman who is very good, and the nurses page you exactly as often as before.

events.title: The Fourth Floor
events.body: She is nine and she has been on the pediatric oncology floor, on and off, for two years, and she knows the nurses' children's names and the vending machine's moods and which chaplain will play cards. That is you. This week the treatment has stopped, and her parents have been told, and they have told her nothing, and they have asked you not to. The father says that she is a child and should have her last weeks without fear. The mother says nothing and looks at the window. She has asked you, this afternoon, with the cards on the blanket, whether she is going to die, in the tone she uses for asking whether it will snow, and she is looking at you, and she is a person who knows when she is lied to, because she has been lied to by professionals for two years and has learned the signs. The father is in the doorway. She is waiting. The cards are on the blanket and it is your turn.

choices.label: Tell her the truth, in the words a child can hold, and let the father do what he will
choices.outcome: You say yes, probably, and that you do not know when, and that she will not be alone, and she nods as if you had confirmed the snow. She asks what it is like and you say you do not know, and she says that is fair. The father takes you into the corridor and says things you deserve. The mother, later, thanks you. The girl asks for you every day after that, and you come, and you play cards.

effects.key: told a child the truth when her father asked him not to

choices.label: Say what the father asked you to say: that the doctors are doing everything, and play the hand
choices.outcome: She looks at you for a moment longer than she needed to, and then plays her card. You have lied to a dying child in her father's hearing, and it was a kind lie, and she knew. She is gentler with you after that, in the way of a child who has decided to protect an adult. She dies three weeks later. The father sends a note. You keep it in a drawer you do not open.

choices.label: Put the cards down, and ask her what she thinks, and let her tell you
choices.outcome: She thinks she is. She has thought so for a month. She wanted to know whether anyone would say it, and you have not said it, and she has said it herself, and that seems to be what she needed. She asks whether God is nice. You say yes. The father in the doorway has heard all of it and does not come in, and later he tells you, unable to look at you, that she has stopped being afraid.

events.title: The Vote
events.body: He is in his third year of theology and he is the best student you have and the seminary loves him: the rector, the bishops who visit, the donors at the gala. He is charming and quick and his Latin is real. You have also, over two years, watched him lie to you three times about small things and get away with it, and you have watched him with the first-year men, the way he finds the anxious one in a group and makes himself necessary to him and then, when he is bored, drops him. Nothing has been reported. Nothing is reportable. It is a pattern, and a pattern is not a fact, and on Thursday the faculty vote on whether to recommend him to his bishop for the diaconate. The rector has said, in the corridor, that he expects it to be unanimous. The man's bishop, who is not yours, has three men in the seminary and a shortage and a fondness for this one. Your own formation reports have been, you notice reading them back, careful. It is Tuesday.

choices.label: Vote no on Thursday, and say why, in the room, with the pattern laid out
choices.outcome: The room is silent for a while. Two other faculty say, slowly, that they have seen some of it. The vote is not unanimous and the rector's letter to the bishop says so, with your reasons attached, and the bishop calls the rector and then calls you, and is cold. The man is ordained a deacon anyway, a year late, and you will never know whether you were right. The seminary knows you will say it.

effects.key: voted no when the room expected yes

choices.label: Vote yes; a pattern is not a fact, and it is not your diocese
choices.outcome: It is unanimous. The rector is pleased. The man is ordained a deacon in the spring and a priest the year after and sends you a card, and you keep it, and you keep the other thing too, in a place where you can see it. Fifteen years later you hear something about him from a priest of that diocese, and it is not what you feared and it is not nothing, and you think about Thursday.

choices.label: Go to the rector before Thursday with the three lies written down, and ask for a year's delay and a specific plan
choices.outcome: The rector reads the page and is annoyed and then is not, because it is specific and dated and he can defend it to a bishop. The vote is deferred. The man gets a pastoral year in a hard parish with a pastor who does not find him charming, and comes back changed, or better at hiding it; the faculty disagree which. His bishop is irritated for a season. The rector begins to send you the difficult files.

events.title: The Rector's Table
events.body: Once a year the rector gives a dinner for the bishops who send men to the seminary, and the faculty are seated among them, and the rector has been clear, in the faculty meeting, about what the dinner is for. Enrollment is down. Two dioceses are considering sending their men elsewhere. The faculty are to be warm, specific, and confident about the formation program, and are not to discuss the departure of the former vice-rector, the state of the roof, or the new document from Rome. You are seated beside {@bishop}, which the rector arranged, and across from a bishop from another province who has had two glasses of wine and asks you, over the fish, in a voice the table can hear, what you actually think of his men. He has four. Two are fine. One is the best in the house and one should not be there, and the bishop knows which is which, and is testing whether you do, and whether you will say.
events.flavorPrompt: The fish course, the rector's instructions, the bishop across the table testing whether the faculty tell the truth.

choices.label: Give him the seminary's line: they are good men, well formed, and the program is strong
choices.outcome: He nods and turns to the bishop beside him and the moment passes. The rector, at the head of the table, relaxes visibly. Enrollment holds. The bishop across the table sends his men elsewhere the following year anyway, for reasons that may or may not have been the fish course. {@bishop}, beside you, says nothing during dinner and, in the car park, says that he had hoped you would say something.

choices.label: Tell him the truth about the four, in a voice the table can hear
choices.outcome: You name no names and everyone at the table knows which two you mean. The bishop across the table puts his glass down and looks at you for a long moment and says thank you, and means it, and the rector at the head of the table does not. Enrollment from that diocese goes up. The rector does not seat you beside anyone important again. {@bishop} tells the story at his own table for a year.

choices.label: Tell him you will happily say it in his office, and ask him what he wants from a seminary in ten years
choices.outcome: He laughs, and answers, at length, and the table gets twenty minutes on what a bishop actually needs from a seminary, which the rector had never thought to ask. The next morning he comes to your office and you tell him about the four, and he already knew. He sends a fifth man the next year. The rector, who saw all of it, begins to think of you as someone who can be seated anywhere.

events.title: The Evaluations
events.body: The course evaluations come back in January in a manila envelope from the academic dean, who has read them first and has attached a note that says only, let's talk. The numbers are fine. The comments are not. Eleven men took your course on the sacraments and seven have written something, and what they have written is that they could not tell what you believed. One says you teach the objections better than the answers. One says you are afraid of the Catechism. One, at length and with footnotes, says that the course was the first time anyone in the building had treated him like an adult, and that he is grateful, and that he has never been so confused. The dean, when you talk, is kind. He says the men are anxious and the bishops are anxious and the seminary is a place where clarity is currency. He would like the course to be, he says, more affirming. He does not say what happens if it is not. He does not need to.
events.flavorPrompt: The manila envelope, the seven comments, the dean's word affirming and the one with footnotes.

choices.label: Change nothing; the one with footnotes is the one you were teaching
choices.outcome: The course runs again as it was, and the evaluations are the same, and the dean's note the following January is shorter. The one with footnotes comes to your office in his diaconate year to say that he has understood it now, all of it, and that he is glad you did not change it. He is the only one who says so. The rector begins to describe you, to bishops, as demanding.

choices.label: Rewrite the course: the answer first, then the objection, then the answer again
choices.outcome: It is a better course for the men who were struggling and a worse one for the one with footnotes, who takes the seminar instead. The evaluations come back warm. The dean is pleased. Two bishops mention to the rector that their men speak well of the sacraments course. You know exactly what was lost and you can name it, and you notice that nobody else can, which is the thing about clarity.

choices.label: Open the first class of the spring with the comments, read aloud, and ask the room what it believes
choices.outcome: It is the most uncomfortable ninety minutes of the year and by the end of it the men have said, out loud, to each other, what they believe about the Eucharist and why, and three of them have said something they did not know they thought. The one who wrote that you were afraid of the Catechism says so to your face and you thank him. The dean hears about it. The evaluations in May are unrecognizable.

events.title: The Grade
events.body: {@bishop} calls on a Tuesday evening and is warm for two minutes and then is not. A seminarian of {diocese}, in his second year of theology, has failed your course in Christology, and the failure has been reported to the diocese in the ordinary way, and the bishop has three men in the seminary and eleven parishes without a resident pastor and a vocations director who is discouraged. He does not ask you to change the grade. He asks whether the grade is really necessary. He says the man is pious, and works hard at the parish placement, and will never be a theologian and does not need to be, and that he, the bishop, has known priests who could not have passed your course and buried half the diocese with grace. All of this is true. It is also true that the man cannot say what the Council of Chalcedon decided or why it matters, and that in three years he will be asked to preach on it. The bishop waits. It is his diocese and it is your course.
events.flavorPrompt: The bishop's two warm minutes and what follows, the eleven parishes, Chalcedon.

choices.label: Hold the grade, and tell him why, kindly, and offer to tutor the man yourself
choices.outcome: There is a silence on the line and then he says that he supposes that is what he sent you there for. The man repeats the course in the summer with you across the table twice a week and passes, honestly, and can say what Chalcedon decided. The bishop does not thank you. He does not need to; he has told the story to the vocations director, who tells it to the next class.

effects.key: held a grade against his own bishop

choices.label: Offer a re-examination in two weeks, oral, and let the man show what he can do
choices.outcome: He passes the oral, barely, because an oral is kinder than a paper and because you are, and the grade is amended. The bishop is grateful and says so. The academic dean notices the amendment and says nothing, in the way of a man filing something. The man is ordained on time and is a good pastor and never once preaches on Chalcedon, which may be for the best.

choices.label: Tell him, as one priest to another, exactly what the man cannot do and what it will cost a parish
choices.outcome: You talk for forty minutes, and it is not about the grade; it is about what a priest needs to know and what he can do without, and the bishop has opinions and so do you. He keeps the failure. He asks you to write him a page on what the seminary should be doing about men like this, and you do, and it goes to the rector with his name on it. The man passes in the summer.

events.title: In the Internal Forum
events.body: He knocks at nine at night, which the men do not do, and asks whether he can speak to you in the internal forum, which means that what he says cannot leave the room and cannot go into any report you write. He is a second-year man, steady, unremarkable, the kind the rector never worries about. He sits down and says that he has not believed in God since October. Not the priesthood; he can imagine the priesthood. God. He has kept going to chapel and saying the Office and serving Mass and none of it has been anything, and he has told no one, and he has read what the books say about dryness and does not think this is that. He asks you whether you have ever. He is not asking for a lecture on the dark night. He is asking whether the man across the desk from him, who has been a priest for years and teaches him the sacraments, has ever sat where he is sitting. He is looking at you. The door is shut.

choices.label: Tell him the truth about your own worst year, and what you did with it
choices.outcome: You tell him, plainly, without making it a story with a moral, and he listens the way a man listens who has been told something true for the first time in months. He does not leave the seminary. He does not stop doubting either, for a long time. He comes back on Thursdays. Years later he is a pastor and you hear that his confessional has a line, and you think you know why.

choices.label: Tell him, gently, that this is for his spiritual director, and walk him to that door
choices.outcome: It is the correct answer and he knows it is and he goes. His director is a good priest and does what directors do. The man stays another year and then leaves quietly in the summer, and the rector's note says he discerned out. He sends you a Christmas card from a job in insurance. You did nothing wrong, and it will be a while before you can say that sentence without hearing the other half of it.

choices.label: Take him through it: what the tradition actually says about the absence of God, and who has said it
choices.outcome: You take a book off the shelf and then another, and it is midnight before you stop, and he leaves with three of them under his arm and something that is not faith but is not nothing. He reads all three. He argues with you about one of them for a term. It becomes, without either of you deciding it, spiritual direction of a kind, and it lasts until he is ordained, believing, he says, about four days a week.

events.title: The Document
events.body: Rome has issued a document on the liturgy, and the faculty meeting on Tuesday is about how the seminary will teach it, which is the polite way of saying which half of the faculty will win. One half reads it as a correction and wants it in the syllabus by Lent, verbatim, with the men taught to celebrate accordingly. The other half reads it as a document, one among many, to be taught in context and with the history that produced it, which is the polite way of saying taught with the objections. The rector, who would like to retire without a letter from anyone's bishop, wants a vote. The men know the meeting is happening. Some of them have already decided which professors are on which side and have said so in the refectory. You teach the sacraments. Whatever you say on Tuesday will be in a seminarian's email to his bishop by Wednesday, and the bishops who read those emails include {@bishop}, whose views on the document you can guess.
events.flavorPrompt: The Tuesday meeting, the two halves of the faculty, the refectory that has already decided, the email to a bishop.

choices.label: Vote for the syllabus by Lent, verbatim, and say that the men should learn to obey a document before they learn to argue with one
choices.outcome: It carries by two votes. The document is in the syllabus by Lent. The other half of the faculty is cool with you for a year and then is not, because faculties forget. A bishop who agrees with the document mentions you to another bishop. {@bishop} hears your name in the sentence. The men on the losing side of the refectory do not take your seminar. The men on the winning side do, and some are the wrong reason.

choices.label: Vote to teach it in context, with the history, and say that a priest who cannot explain a document cannot defend it
choices.outcome: It fails by two votes, and the document goes in verbatim, and you teach it in context anyway, in your own course, which nobody can stop. A seminarian's email reaches his bishop by Wednesday, as expected. Two bishops ask the rector about you and the rector, to his credit, says you are a fine teacher. {@bishop} is one of the two. He does not say what he thinks.

choices.label: Propose a joint seminar: one professor from each half, in the same room, in front of the men, for a term
choices.outcome: The rector seizes on it, because it is a vote he does not have to hold. The seminar is oversubscribed. The two professors, who have not spoken in a year, discover they can disagree in front of thirty men without either of them dying, and the men discover the same. Bishops hear that the seminary teaches the document seriously and from every side. The rector begins to think of you as the person who ends meetings.

events.title: The Alumnus
events.body: He was two years ahead of you in this building, and you served his first Mass, and now he is a bishop, eight months consecrated, of a diocese in another province, and he has come back to give the Lenten day of recollection because the rector asked and because a new bishop goes where he is asked. He is good at it. In the afternoon, between the conferences, he finds you in your office and shuts the door and stops being a bishop for twenty minutes. He wants to know what the seminary has become. Not the brochure: the faculty, the men, whether the formation is real or a performance for visiting bishops, whether he should send his own men here or somewhere else. He says he is asking you because you were never a liar. He also, at the end, mentions that he has a diocese with no one in it he trusts, and that he remembers you, and leaves that where it is. The bell goes for the next conference. He has to give it.
events.flavorPrompt: The bishop who was a seminarian here, the door shut for twenty minutes, the thing left where it is.

choices.label: Tell him the truth about the seminary, all of it, the roof and the vice-rector and the two halves
choices.outcome: He listens without writing anything down, which is how you know he is remembering it. He sends his men here anyway, two of them, with a note to the rector that says what he expects. The rector, who guesses where the note came from, is cool with you until the two men turn out well. The bishop writes to you at Christmas. The letter has one sentence in it about the future and you read it several times.

choices.label: Give him the brochure, warmly, and let him find out for himself; he is a bishop now, and you are faculty
choices.outcome: He knows the brochure when he hears it and does not press, being a bishop now and used to it. He sends his men elsewhere. The rector never knows there was a conversation. The Christmas card is a card. Years later, when his name comes up in {diocese} for a reason you cannot foresee, you will remember the twenty minutes and the door and the thing he left where it was.

choices.label: Tell him the truth in five sentences, and then ask him for something: a summer in his diocese for your best two men
choices.outcome: He laughs, because nobody has asked him for anything in eight months that was not money, and says yes before you have finished. The two men spend a summer in his hardest parish and come back different. He sends three of his own men here the year after. The rector is delighted and does not know why. The bishop, at his next visit, asks after you by name in front of the rector, which is a sentence in itself.

events.title: Your Signature
events.body: The formation report goes to the man's bishop in April with the signatures of the whole formation team on the last page, and the one on your desk is for a seminarian of {diocese}, in his final year, and it says that the team has no concerns. You have one. He is rigid in a way that is not piety, and in the practice homilies he preaches at people rather than to them, and twice in the pastoral placement the parish secretary has called the seminary to ask, carefully, whether he is all right. None of it is disqualifying. All of it is the kind of thing a bishop would want to know about a man he is going to ordain in June. The rector has read the draft and signed it, and says the concern belongs in the verbal report, which he will give, and that a written paragraph follows a man for life. He is not wrong. The vocations director of {diocese} is a friend of the man's family. {@bishop} will read whatever is on the page and nothing that is not.

choices.label: Sign it as written, and trust the rector's verbal report to carry what the page does not
choices.outcome: You sign. The rector gives the verbal report, and it is careful, and the bishop hears it as a rector being careful. The man is ordained in June.
