He is a difficult curate and a worse pastor, and in his fourth year a parish council writes to the bishop, and the bishop pulls the file and finds a page that says no concerns, with your name on it. He does not call you about it. He does not need to.

choices.label: Add your paragraph, specific and fair, and sign under it, and let the rector do what he likes with his own signature
choices.outcome: The rector reads it and removes his own signature and adds a covering note that says the team was not unanimous. The bishop reads both and calls the vocations director and then calls you. The man is ordained a deacon and given a year in a parish with a pastor who was told what to watch for, and is ordained a priest the year after, having been watched. The rector does not forgive the note for a while.

effects.key: put his concern on the page and signed under it

choices.label: Sign the report as written, and write the bishop a letter of your own, by hand, the same day
choices.outcome: The letter is two pages and says exactly what you saw and when. The bishop reads it before the report and calls the rector, who is caught between a clean page and a letter he did not know existed, and is angry, and cannot say so. The man gets his extra year. The rector learns that the faculty write to bishops. The bishop learns that you do, and begins to ask you about other men.

events.title: Defender of the Bond
events.body: The tribunal internship is mostly reading, and this week the judicial vicar gives you something to write: the defender of the bond's observations on a nullity case that everyone in the building would like to see go through. The petitioner is the son of a family that has paid for two wings of {school} and a chapel at {residence}. The grounds are the usual grounds. The evidence is thin in one place, which you find on the second reading: the psychological expert's report leans on a single interview, and the respondent, who lives in Ohio and did not answer the tribunal's letters, has never been heard. The defender of the bond's job is to say so. It is also a job that is done, in a busy tribunal, in a paragraph that says the bond has been adequately defended and the court may proceed. The judicial vicar has not told you which kind of paragraph he wants. He has told you it is due Friday, and that the family's pastor has called twice.
events.flavorPrompt: The case everyone wants to go through, the single interview, the respondent in Ohio who never answered.

choices.label: Write the observations as the office requires: the thin place named, the respondent's silence, the court asked to wait
choices.outcome: The judicial vicar reads it, and reads it again, and says it is correct and that he wishes it were not. The case is delayed four months while the respondent is found and heard. She has a great deal to say. The decree is affirmative anyway, in the end, and is unassailable, and the family's pastor stops calling. The judicial vicar tells the tribunal at home that you can write a brief.

choices.label: Write the paragraph, the usual one, and let the court proceed; the outcome would be the same
choices.outcome: It goes through in six weeks and the family is grateful and the chapel at {residence} gets new kneelers. The judicial vicar signs it without comment. You have learned what the tribunal does when it is busy and who it is busy for, and you have been part of it, and it is not a sin and it is not the office either. The respondent in Ohio never knows there was a case.

choices.label: Ask the judicial vicar for a week, find the respondent yourself, and take her testimony by rogatory
choices.outcome: She is in Dayton and answers the phone on the first try, and has been waiting eleven years for someone to ask. The testimony is taken through the Cincinnati tribunal in three weeks. The case is stronger for it and goes through, and the defender's observations are a page and clean. The judicial vicar says nothing about it for a month, and then gives you the next hard file, and the one after.

events.title: The Convention
events.body: The canon law society meets in October in a hotel with bad carpet, and the students from {school} go because their professors go and because it is where the judicial vicars of the country hire. The plenary on the second morning is a famous canonist, a monsignor with a chair and a book, on the bishop's discretion in penal process, and his argument is that the norms have taken too much from the bishop and given it to procedure, and that a bishop who cannot act on his own judgment is not a father. He is a good speaker. Half the room is nodding. The other half, which includes the judicial vicar you intern for, is very still. There is a question period. Your seminar paper this term is on exactly this, and it says the opposite, and your professor, who is in the third row, has turned around to look at you. There is a microphone in the aisle. Two hundred canonists, most of whom will be hiring or recommending someone in the next five years, are in the room.
events.flavorPrompt: The hotel with bad carpet, the monsignor's argument, the professor in the third row who has turned around.

choices.label: Go to the microphone, and put the case from your paper to him, in three minutes, with the canons cited
choices.outcome: He answers you for five minutes and the room is quiet for all of it, and the exchange is the thing people talk about at the reception. Your professor is glad. The judicial vicar is glad. The monsignor, at the reception, buys you a drink and says that you are wrong and that he would like to read the paper. Three judicial vicars ask for your name. One of them is from a diocese you will hear from again.

choices.label: Say nothing in the plenary, and give the paper in the student session that afternoon to whoever comes
choices.outcome: Eleven people come, which is good for the student session, and two of them are judicial vicars and one is the monsignor's assistant, who takes notes. The paper is good. The questions are real. Nobody at the reception talks about it, and the monsignor never learns your name, and the two judicial vicars do, and write it down, which is what the afternoon session is for.

choices.label: Stay in your seat, listen, and learn how a man with a chair argues a thing you think is wrong
choices.outcome: You take four pages of notes and the notes are better than the paper you had written, and you rewrite the paper over the winter with his argument in it, answered. Your professor is briefly disappointed and then is not. Nobody in the room learns your name. The paper is the best thing you write at {school}, and the judicial vicar at home reads it two years later and remembers it.

events.title: The Senator
events.body: The party is in a house in Georgetown with a garden, given by a Catholic couple who collect priests the way other people collect paintings, and you are there because a classmate at {school} was asked to bring someone young. There is a senator. He is Catholic, from a state that is not yours, and he has voted for years in a way that the bishops of his state have written letters about, on the death penalty most recently, and he has had three glasses of something good. He finds you by the fireplace, and six people find the two of you, and he asks, in a voice built for rooms like this, what the Church actually thinks of him. He is smiling. He has asked this of priests before and enjoyed the answers. The six people are two journalists, a Jesuit, the host, and two people whose names you did not catch. He is waiting. The Jesuit is looking at his shoes. You are a student priest from {diocese} with a collar on and a glass in your hand, and the room has gone quiet enough to hear.
events.flavorPrompt: The Georgetown garden, the senator by the fireplace, the six listeners, the Jesuit looking at his shoes.

choices.label: Tell him, in the room, what the Church thinks about the death penalty and about a Catholic who votes for it
choices.outcome: You say it in four sentences, courteously, with the Catechism's own words in it, and the senator's smile does not move and his eyes do. One of the journalists writes something down. The Jesuit looks up. The host is delighted, because it is the best thing that has happened at her parties in years. The clip does not run, because there is no clip, but the sentence does, and it reaches {diocese} in a week.

choices.label: Tell him you would be glad to say, and that you will say it to him and not to the room, and give him your number
choices.outcome: He laughs, and the room laughs, and the moment passes, and the host is faintly disappointed. He calls, which you did not expect, on a Tuesday, and you talk for an hour, and it is not the conversation the fireplace would have got. He does not change his vote. He goes to confession, somewhere, to someone, and you will never know whether that was the hour. The journalists have nothing to write.

choices.label: Give him the paragraph number, cheerfully, and ask him about the Nationals
choices.outcome: He knows the paragraph number, as it turns out, and quotes it, and the two of you talk baseball for ten minutes and the six people drift away. The Jesuit says, later, that it was nicely done. It was. It was also nothing, and you know it was nothing, and a student priest who says nothing at a Georgetown party is exactly what {diocese} sent, and is remembered by no one in the room.

events.title: East of the River
events.body: The pastor is seventy-four and has been east of the river for twenty-six years, and his parish is a Black Catholic parish with a gospel choir and a Mass that runs two hours and a church that was full in 1985 and is half full now, and he needs a priest for the ten-thirty. He got your name from the tribunal. He does not want a student who will say Mass and leave. He says so on the phone. He wants a priest who will stay for the coffee and learn the names and preach a homily that the choir can answer, and he is aware that {school} does not teach that, and that you are from {diocese}, which he has never been to and does not need to. He offers you the ten-thirty every Sunday until you go home. The canon law seminar meets Monday mornings, which after a two-hour Mass and a coffee hour and a drive across the city is a different Monday. The students at {residence} who supply in Northern Virginia are home by one.
events.flavorPrompt: The pastor's phone call, the two-hour Mass, the choir that answers a homily, the different Monday.

choices.label: Take every Sunday, stay for the coffee, learn the names
choices.outcome: It takes until Advent to learn to preach so that the choir answers, and when it happens the first time you nearly stop. Mondays are hard. The seminar notices. By Lent the ushers call you by your first name and the pastor lets you do a funeral, and by the time you go home you have been a parish priest in a way {diocese} has not yet asked of you. The degree takes a little longer.

choices.label: Offer him one Sunday a month, honestly, and Northern Virginia for the rest
choices.outcome: He says one a month is not a priest, it is a visitor, and takes it anyway, because he has no one else. You are a visitor. The choir is kind to you and does not answer the homily. Northern Virginia is easy and pays well and you are home by one. The pastor sends you a card when you go home, addressed to Father, with no first name, and you understand what it says.

choices.label: Take every Sunday, and ask the choir director to teach you how a homily is preached in that church
choices.outcome: She is sixty and has buried three pastors and says she will try. It is the most useful instruction in preaching you will ever receive and none of it is in a book. By Easter the church answers you, and you answer back, and the pastor sits in the sanctuary with his eyes shut and his hand moving. When you go home you preach differently, and the people of {diocese} notice, and cannot say what it is.

effects.key: learned to preach east of the river

events.title: Massachusetts Avenue
events.body: {@random_classmate} has been lent to the nunciature for a year, which happens to a priest of {diocese} perhaps once a generation, and he asks you to dinner at a restaurant near the building with a tablecloth and no prices. He is well. He has a car and a driver some days and he has learned to say nothing in the way they say it there. Over the second course he says that the nunciature is preparing something on {diocese}, the ordinary kind of thing, a picture of the place, and that he has been asked to contribute what he knows, and that he would like to know what you know. About {@bishop}. About the chancery, the money, the man who left, the morale of the priests. He says it is not an investigation. He says that the picture will be drawn whether or not it is accurate, and that a son of the diocese at the table is a chance for it to be accurate. He is your classmate. He is also, for this year, the nunciature. The waiter has taken the plates.

choices.label: Tell him what you know, all of it, as accurately as you can
choices.outcome: You talk for two hours and he asks good questions and writes nothing down. Whatever goes into the picture, it is accurate. Some of it is not flattering to {@bishop}, and some of it is, and you have no way of knowing which parts the nunciature keeps. A year later a monsignor in Rome knows your name. Two years later, at a deanery dinner, a priest who should not know says that you talk to the nunciature.

choices.label: Tell him you are a student priest and that {diocese} has a bishop with a telephone
choices.outcome: He takes it well, being your classmate, and less well, being the nunciature. The dinner ends early. The picture is drawn without you, from whoever else they asked, and you will never know how it came out. He does not ask again. When he comes home the following year he is friendly with you in the way of a man who remembers a dinner, and a little careful.

choices.label: Say nothing at the table, and call the bishop the next morning to tell him what is being asked
choices.outcome: He is quiet on the line for a while and then says he had wondered, and thanks you, and asks two questions about what exactly was said. He does not ask you to do anything. He handles it, in whatever way bishops handle the nunciature. Your classmate never learns of the call, or learns and says nothing, which at the nunciature is the same thing. The bishop remembers who told him.
